chapters.title: The World of the Norse Gods

pages.text: The Norse gods lived in a universe of nine worlds, connected by an enormous tree called Yggdrasil, the World Tree. At the top of the universe was Asgard, home of the Aesir gods. At the bottom was Niflheim, a realm of ice and mist. In between were worlds of giants, dwarves, elves, and humans. The whole universe was alive, and it was temporary: the Norse myths end with Ragnarok, the destruction of everything, from which only a few survivors emerge to begin the world again.

image.note: Illustration: Yggdrasil the World Tree with the nine worlds shown in its branches and roots

pages.text: The chief Norse god was Odin, the All-Father. He sacrificed one of his eyes to drink from the Well of Wisdom and acquire knowledge. He hung himself from Yggdrasil for nine days to learn the runes, the magical writing system. Odin was not a comfortable god of warmth and plenty. He was a god of wisdom, war, death, poetry, and magic, and he paid a price for every piece of knowledge he gained.

His son Thor was the most popular of the Norse gods, because he was the most straightforward: powerful, loyal, honest, and protective of humanity. He carried a hammer called Mjolnir, which always returned to his hand when thrown. He drove a chariot pulled by two goats across the sky, and the thunder that followed was the sound of the wheels. When lightning struck, Thor had thrown his hammer.
Thor woke one morning to find his hammer missing. Without Mjolnir, Asgard was defenceless against the frost giants. He searched everywhere. His hammer was gone.

image.note: Illustration: Thor looking under furniture in his vast hall, increasingly frustrated

pages.text: A message arrived. The frost giant Thrym had stolen the hammer. He would return it on one condition: Freya, the most beautiful of the goddesses, must become his wife. Freya refused so furiously that the gods around her trembled. Loki, the trickster, proposed an alternative: Thor himself would disguise himself as a bride, travel to Thrym's hall, and retrieve the hammer. Thor, who was not known for his enthusiasm for disguises, objected. Loki pointed out that without the hammer, the giants would take Asgard. Thor put on a dress.

At the wedding feast, Thrym became suspicious. His bride ate an entire ox, eight salmon, and all the food set aside for the women, and drank three barrels of mead. Loki, disguised as the bride's handmaid, explained that the bride had been so excited about the wedding that she hadn't eaten for eight days. When Thrym placed Mjolnir in the bride's lap to bless the marriage, Thor seized it, killed Thrym and all his relatives, and returned home. He did not discuss the episode afterwards.

There is a tale of how Thor's hammer was made, and of the trickster's part in it. Loki, for mischief, had cut off the golden hair of Thor's wife, and to save himself he promised her hair of real gold, made by the dwarves. The dwarves, master smiths, made not only the golden hair but a ship that folded into a pocket, a spear that never missed, and, greatest of all, the hammer Mjollnir, whose handle was a little short because Loki, in fly form, had bitten the smith as he worked.

Short handle or not, Mjollnir became the mightiest weapon in all the nine worlds, able to level mountains and return to Thor's hand when thrown. So the gods gained their greatest defence through Loki's mischief and the dwarves' craft. This is very like the Norse world: good and ill are tangled together, the trickster's wrongdoing produces the gods' salvation, and nothing, not even a magic hammer, is quite perfect.

Loki was the most complex of the Norse gods. He was the son of a giant but was accepted among the Aesir. He was brilliant, charming, and creative. He was also a shapeshifter and a liar, and his cleverness caused as much trouble as it solved.

image.note: Illustration: Loki in half-shadow, a mischievous expression, in human form

pages.text: Loki had three children with a giantess: the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jormungandr, and the half-dead, half-living figure of Hel. The gods, alarmed by prophecies about these children, took action. Jormungandr was thrown into the ocean surrounding the world, where he grew so large that he could encircle the earth and bite his own tail. Hel was sent to rule the realm of the dead. Fenrir was bound with a magical chain that he could not break.

At Ragnarok, Fenrir will break free. Jormungandr will rise from the ocean. Hel will send her armies. Loki himself will fight against the gods. The Norse myths hold this ending constantly in view, and find in it not despair but something more interesting: the idea that knowing you will eventually lose does not mean you stop fighting. The gods of Asgard know Ragnarok is coming. They fight anyway.

Odin hungered for wisdom. He went to the Well of Mimír, a spring that contained the knowledge of all things. Mimír, the guardian of the well, told him the price: one of Odin's eyes. Odin pulled out his eye and dropped it into the well. He drank.

image.note: Illustration: Odin at the Well of Mimír, hand raised to his eye, expression of absolute resolution

pages.text: In the Norse myths, wisdom always came at a cost. Odin paid the highest one. He then sought the runes, the magical writing of the Norse world that gave power over fate itself. To obtain them, Odin hung himself from Yggdrasil, wounded by his own spear, without food, without water, for nine days and nine nights. On the ninth night, he looked down and saw the runes in the darkness below him. He grasped them and fell.

Odin gave up his eye. He gave up comfort. He gave up safety. He gave up physical wholeness. What he gained was knowledge. The Norse myth of Odin is a myth about the cost of wisdom, and it does not pretend the cost is small.

The Norse myths know how the story ends. At Ragnarok, the forces of chaos will overcome the gods. Thor will fight Jormungandr and kill the serpent, then die from its venom. Odin will be swallowed by Fenrir. Loki and Heimdall will kill each other. The world will burn and sink into the sea.

image.note: Illustration: the battlefield of Ragnarok, gods and monsters locked in combat against a burning sky

pages.text: Then the earth will rise from the water again, green and fertile. A man and a woman, hidden in the World Tree during the destruction, will emerge and repopulate the earth. A new sun will rise. Some of the gods' children will survive.

The Norse myths do not promise that good will permanently defeat evil. They promise something more honest: that the fight matters, even when you know you will eventually lose it. That courage is not dependent on certainty of victory. That after the worst imaginable destruction, something will survive and begin again.

What are we to make of a religion whose gods know they are doomed? The Norse did not flinch from it. Their gods are brave, flawed, and mortal in spirit if not in years, and they face an ending they cannot escape. Yet they do not despair, and they do not surrender. They feast, they fight, they keep their word, and when Ragnarok comes they will meet it with weapons in hand. To the people who told these tales, that was the whole point.

The lesson the Norse drew was a hard and bracing one: courage is not the belief that you will win. It is doing what is right even when you know you will lose. A warrior could not choose the day of his death, they believed, but he could choose how he met it. In a cold and dangerous world, that was a faith worth having, and something of its iron has passed down the centuries into every story of heroes who fight on against hopeless odds.
